newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan students blame woes on outside powers.
newsitem.headline: Afghan students blame woes on outside powers.

text.p: Foreign intervention has turned Afghanistan into a vast killing field where a whole generation has known only war, university students in the Uzbek stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif complained on Tuesday.
"Don't ask us about politics, don't ask us about Taleban. We are interested in life and education, not death and war," 24-year-old student Nasir Bessed spat out at reporters.

"Everyone wants to know what we think about the Taleban, but they are not an Afghan creation. They were created by Pakistan and the United States. Russia, Iran, Pakistan, America -- they say they want to help Afghanistan but all they do is help Afghans make war."
Nasir spoke at the University of Mazar-i-Sharif, one of five institutions of higher education still operating in Afghanistan.
He and his fellow students did little to hide their annoyance at Western fascination with the Taleban forces who captured Kabul 10 days ago and imposed rigid Islamic law on the city.

Women in Kabul have been banned from working or even leaving the house unless covered from head-to-foot and accompanied by a male relative. Men have been ordered to grow beards and pray five times a day at a mosque rather than at home.

Life in the Uzbek stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif -- about 400 kilometres (250 miles) northwest of Kabul near the border with Uzbekistan -- is considerably more relaxed but people fear that war could spread north and engulf them.
General Abdul Rashid Dostum, the Uzbek warlord whose picture is everywhere in this city, recently warned the Taleban he would fight them if they continue to press northwards.
At the university, most students shrug off any mention of the Taleban and focus on practical problems like education and finding employment.
"If you would write that we have no text-books in our classrooms and no proper laboratories it would be better than writing about the Taleban," said 28-year-old Hussein Ahmadi, an English student.

"All the reporters want to know about Taleban, but for us it is really nothing new. It is just more of the war we have known for 18 years. I will graduate in two months and I will have no job because the war has wrecked my country."
The dozen or so men in Hussein's class sit at the back of the room but press forward to speak at the first opportunity.
"It's true I am not political since I am a student, but my education will be wasted if the Taleban come to Mazar-i-Sharif," said 21-year-old Maria, who fled Kabul with her family in 1992.

"I want to be a teacher. Most of us women in this class do. But under the Taleban that would not be possible. I had hoped to return to Kabul but I would never go back now unless things change. Life is hard in Afghanistan for an educated person, especially a woman."

The talk among shopkeepers and taxi-drivers in this city's dusty bazaars is that Uzbeks and Tajiks in the north will join forces to halt the Pashtun-dominated Taleban from advancing. But some university students bristled at the notion of ethnic politics.

"Uzbek, Tajik, Pashtun -- these are labels which mean nothing. We are all Afghans and we could live in peace if outside countries would stop raising these racial and tribal and lingual differences which keep us at war," said Nasir Bessed.
"We get such big promises from outside countries. But they write their promises on ice and then set them in the sun."
